title: Jeremiah 49:34–39
context: The narrator dates this word of the LORD to Jeremiah concerning Elam to the beginning of Zedekiah’s reign. Elam was a people and region east of Babylon, commonly associated with the area around Susa (compare Daniel 8:2), and known for its archers (compare Isaiah 22:6). The LORD of Armies says he will break the bow of Elam, the chief of its strength, scatter its people to the four winds, bring his fierce anger on them, and set his throne in Elam, removing its king and princes. The text does not give details of how or when this happens. The unit ends with a promise that in the latter days the LORD will reverse the captivity of Elam, alongside similar words to Egypt, Moab, and Ammon (46:26; 48:47; 49:6). Some readers also note that Elamites are among those present at Pentecost (Acts 2:9), as a later echo rather than a fulfillment the text claims. Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the passage as shared ground about God’s justice over the nations and his mercy that reaches beyond judgment.

verses.text: The LORD’s word that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning Elam, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the narrator dating the LORD’s word concerning Elam to the beginning of Zedekiah’s reign. Jeremiah’s ministry addresses distant nations too.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Jeremiah’s calling over the nations (compare Jeremiah 1:10). Both traditions commonly read the verse as setting the oracle in history.

verses.text: “The LORD of Armies says: ‘Behold, I will break the bow of Elam, the chief of their might.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD of Armies saying he will break the bow of Elam, the chief of its might. Its greatest strength will fail.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God overturning the source of Elam’s confidence (compare Isaiah 22:6). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober word about human strength.

verses.text: I will bring on Elam the four winds from the four quarters of the sky, and will scatter them toward all those winds. There will be no nation where the outcasts of Elam will not come.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD bringing the four winds against Elam and scattering its people to every nation. The dispersion is wide.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s control over the movements of peoples. Both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, within the oracle’s historical frame.

verses.text: I will cause Elam to be dismayed before their enemies, and before those who seek their life. I will bring evil on them, even my fierce anger,’ says the LORD; ‘and I will send the sword after them, until I have consumed them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying he will dismay Elam before its enemies and bring his fierce anger on them. Judgment is serious.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s righteous anger against the nations. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, as part of the oracle’s announcement of judgment.

verses.text: I will set my throne in Elam, and will destroy from there king and princes,’ says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying he will set his throne in Elam and remove its king and princes. God’s rule replaces human power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an image of God’s sovereignty established over a foreign land. Both traditions commonly read the verse as declaring that God rules over every nation.

verses.text: ‘But it will happen in the latter days that I will reverse the captivity of Elam,’ says the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD promising that in the latter days he will reverse the captivity of Elam. Judgment is not his last word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same promise alongside 46:26, 48:47, and 49:6. Readers in both traditions commonly hold this as shared ground about God’s mercy to the nations.
